source.title: A Signal Propagation Perspective for Pruning Neural Networks at Initialization
source.authors: Namhoon Lee; Thalaiyasingam Ajanthan; S. Gould; P. Torr

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares initialization and signal-propagation conditions and reports their effect on training behavior in pruned networks. This bears on the initialization and trainability aspect of V4, but does not test plain-network depth or training classification error as described in V1.
record.gate_note: Training-loss curves for pruned networks are figure-only. Generalization-error tables are not training-error results and are not included as rows. Results about connection-sensitivity reliability and pruning quality do not directly measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study tests V4's signal-preserving initialization and training-speed relationship in a new setting: sparse networks. Its own SGD training-loss comparisons show faster learning after approximate isometry is restored before training.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: layerwise dynamical isometry improves connection-sensitivity reliability; pruning can damage signal propagation and slow training; restoring approximate orthogonality improves sparse-network trainability. The authors also find that topology and parameter count matter beyond signal propagation and caution that isometry may not persist during training.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies pruning at initialization and subsequent training of sparse networks, including approximate-isometry recovery. It does not reproduce the cited plain-network initialization or depth experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Training behavior varies with pruning method, sparsity, initialization, and approximate-isometry recovery; the text reports these comparisons primarily in figures.

fits_no_version.finding: Poorly conditioned initial Jacobians cause unreliable connection sensitivity and catastrophic pruning failures in the seven-layer tanh MLP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization affects the reliability of connection-sensitivity pruning and whether pruning disconnects a network.

fits_no_version.finding: The classification tables report generalization errors, including comparisons of initialization, supervised versus unsupervised pruning, and architecture sculpting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Signal-propagation-aware pruning can improve sparse-network generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: With approximate isometry enforced, connection-sensitivity-pruned MLPs train faster than randomly pruned MLPs, and dense tanh MLPs still converge faster than the repaired sparse networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse topology and parameter count affect training speed beyond initial signal propagation.

record.problems: Training behavior comparisons are shown in figures without numerical values in the text. Most reported classification results are generalization errors, not training classification errors. The paper notes that two-stage orthogonalization may be suboptimal at high sparsity and that dynamical isometry may not persist during training.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were extracted: the training-loss outcomes relevant to V4 are presented in figures without textual numerical results, and the other tables report generalization errors or pruning and signal-propagation measurements rather than the training-error outcomes specified by the versions.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random or corrupted labels, and its dependence on model size or training recipe.
Spurious local minima in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and the effect of extra student neurons.
Training degradation with depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts.
Maximum trainable depth; very deep tanh networks; orthogonal versus Gaussian weights at matched variance; and training 10,000-layer plain CNNs.
Training relative to initial or evolving stability thresholds, curvature dynamics, and divergence.
Controlled normalization versus no-normalization training-speed or learning-rate comparisons, and Fixup.

missing.what: Record the qualitative before/after isometry-restoration training-speed comparisons for sparse MLPs. The declared figure-only omission overlooks explicit prose reporting significant speed improvements.
missing.locator: Section 4, Figure 2 and accompanying findings; Appendix C, Figures 4 and 7

missing.what: Record the VGG16 comparison without batch normalization: Frobenius restoration dramatically improves training speed, spectral restoration also improves it but less, and Frobenius restoration exceeds dense-network speed early in training. These outcomes are stated explicitly in the caption.

record.verdict_notes: No rows exist to correct. Exact curve values cannot be recovered reliably from the supplied text, but explicit qualitative training comparisons support verdicts. Generalization errors and Jacobian statistics alone do not establish training-speed effects. The study is not an original source for V4.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, and comparisons involving model size, early stopping, or regularization.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual networks as a depth comparison, including whether identity shortcuts prevent higher training error.

The results concern pruned networks and signal propagation; the text does not report numerical training-speed outcomes in extractable text or tables. It does not test plain-network trainable depth or compare orthogonal and Gaussian initialization at matched variance in the specific very-deep tanh or 10,000-layer CNN settings.
Learning rates above stability limits, loss increases and curvature changes, sharpness, or divergence.
Batch normalization versus no normalization as a training-speed or learning-rate-tolerance comparison. Batch normalization is removed in one experiment, without a reported BN-versus-no-BN result.

relationships.condition: Seven-layer sparse MLPs on MNIST, with linear, tanh, ReLU, or leaky-ReLU activations
relationships.reason: Based on Section 4 and Figures 2, 4, and 7, rather than extracted rows: restoring approximate isometry before training improves signal propagation and accelerates loss reduction compared with the corresponding pruned networks without restoration.
relationships.display_finding: Restoring approximate isometry before training improved signal propagation and accelerated loss reduction relative to pruned networks without restoration.

source_check.condition: Seven-layer sparse MLPs on MNIST, with linear, tanh, ReLU, or leaky-ReLU activations
source_check.reason: Section 4 and Figures 2 and 4 report improved signal propagation and faster training after approximate-isometry restoration. Figure 7 explicitly extends the conclusion to ReLU and leaky-ReLU.

relationships.condition: Sparse VGG16 on CIFAR-10 without batch normalization
relationships.reason: Based on Figure 8's caption, rather than extracted rows: both Frobenius- and spectral-norm isometry restoration accelerate training relative to broken isometry; Frobenius restoration produces the greater improvement.
relationships.display_finding: Both Frobenius- and spectral-norm isometry restoration accelerated training, with Frobenius restoration producing the greater improvement.
